concept.name: Dealer market
concept.definition: A market structure in which dealers (market makers) stand ready to buy and sell from their own inventory at publicly quoted prices, so customers transact with a dealer as counterparty rather than directly with one another.
concept.intuition: Instead of trading with the person on the other side, you always trade with a shopkeeper who quotes a price to buy and a price to sell.
concept.mechanics: Dealers post or respond to requests with bid and ask quotes, profit from the bid-ask spread and inventory management, and internalize customer order flow; inter-dealer trading lets them lay off unwanted positions.
concept.failure_modes: Dealer liquidity is commitment-optional in stress: dealers widen quotes or withdraw when inventory risk spikes, and opaque, bilateral pricing can leave customers unsure whether they received a fair price.
concept.misconceptions: Dealers are not obligated to lose money providing liquidity — outside formal market maker obligations, they quote when it suits them; the spread is compensation for immediacy and inventory risk, not a fixed tax.
concept.example: Corporate bonds trade in a dealer market: a portfolio manager asks several dealers for a bid on a bond position and sells to the highest bidder.
